rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The notables' response launches the Moses-sorcerers contest, also recounted at 20:58–70 and 26:36–48; the Bible gives a brief version in which Aaron casts the staff.
rows.anchor: The reaction of the notables in vv. 109–10 sets up the competition between Moses and the sorcerers of Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contest meditates on prophethood, miracles, and sorcery, distinguishing their causality, power, and reality.
rows.anchor: a meditation on the relationship between prophethood, miracles, and sorcery and the differences between miracles and sorcery

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because disbelievers may dismiss prophetic miracles as sorcery, their primary role is to encourage inwardly receptive or wavering people and distinguish the misguided from the hardened.
rows.anchor: the primary function of these miracles is to encourage belief among those who are already inwardly disposed to it

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Putting Moses and Aaron off means detaining them, either by delaying their departure or imprisoning them.
rows.anchor: is understood to be a suggestion that he detain them by either delaying their departure or imprisoning them (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One report says the marshaled sorcerers boasted of superior skill in manipulating staffs, ropes, and snakes.
rows.anchor: According to one report, the marshaled sorcerers boast of their superior skill in the manipulation of staffs, ropes, and snakes (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Other reports say the marshaled officials sought sorcerers able to produce feats like Moses'.
rows.anchor: other reports indicate that the marshalers sought out sorcerers capable of feats similar to those produced by Moses (IK)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The sorcerers seek a reward for victory, and Pharaoh promises they will join his honored court or inner circle.
rows.anchor: their reward will be that they shall be among those brought nigh, meaning that they will become honored members of his court or his inner circle (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward language is worldly on its face but ambiguously foreshadows spiritual victory: the defeated sorcerers submit to God and will be rewarded by Him.
rows.anchor: their subsequent submission to God and to Moses can be understood as a spiritual “victory,” for which they will surely have a reward with God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's phrase “brought nigh” also describes prophets, angels, and the most righteous in the highest Paradise; the later verses suggest the sorcerers were martyred.
rows.anchor: it is noteworthy that Pharaoh’s promise that they shall be among those brought nigh

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Some commentators see proper etiquette in the sorcerers letting Moses choose who casts first, although they preferred to cast first.
rows.anchor: Some commentators indicate that the sorcerers demonstrated proper etiquette by allowing Moses to choose who should cast the staff first (R, Z), even as they clearly preferred to cast first (Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some commentators say God rewarded the sorcerers' graciousness toward Moses by bringing faith into their hearts.
rows.anchor: Some commentators propose that it is as a reward

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their outward courtesy may reflect inner sincerity and their recognition of Moses' noble character.
rows.anchor: this demonstration of outward etiquette, or adab, toward Moses may have been recounted here, because it suggests that the sorcerers possessed an inner sincerity

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Moses graciously lets them cast first because he understands their wish and trusts God's aid; a miracle has divine cause and cannot be imitated by human agency.
rows.anchor: he understands their desire to do so and because he is certain that God will aid him and that no sorcery can defeat a miracle

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Their casting first lets Moses expose the deception more clearly when his staff devours it.
rows.anchor: the sorcerers’ casting first allows Moses to demonstrate more easily the powerlessness of their deceptions in the face of the truth (IK, R)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The sorcerers bewitched the spectators by slight of hand and illusion; 20:69 calls the feat a sorcerer's trick.
rows.anchor: bewitched the eyes of the people through slight of hand and illusion (Z); see also 20:69

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their spectacle awed the people; the parallel says it made Moses fear inwardly.
rows.anchor: The people were struck with awe by the sorcerers’feats

rows.speaker: IK, R, Z
rows.claim: The sorcerers used painted ropes and wooden staffs to create the illusion of writhing snakes.
rows.anchor: The sorcerers cast ropes and wooden staffs (see 26:44) that were painted so as to create the illusion of writhing snakes

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Other reports say mercury inside the ropes and staffs made them move in the hot sun during an open-desert contest at midday.
rows.anchor: Others report that the sorcerers had placed mercury inside the staffs and ropes so that they began to move in the hot sun

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Moses waits for God's direct instruction to cast his staff, heard only by Moses, showing that God alone wills and empowers the feat.
rows.anchor: he waits until God revealed unto him the direct instruction to cast it—a command heard only by Moses (R, Ṭs)—indicating that the power and will behind this feat belong to God alone

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Moses' staff becomes a serpent and literally swallows the staffs and ropes disguised as serpents, then returns to its former shape when he grasps it.
rows.anchor: this serpent is reported to have literally devoured the sorcerers’ deception, that is, to have swallowed up the staffs and ropes that had been made to look like writhing serpents (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The truth's coming to pass means it became manifest and defeated the tricks, validating Moses' prophethood.
rows.anchor: That the truth came to pass means that it became plainly manifest and victorious over the sorcerers’ deceptions (Ṭ) and that Moses’ prophethood was validated (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Because waqaʿa can mean fall or alight, some suggest the truth alighted on the sorcerers' hearts before they submitted.
rows.anchor: some have suggested that here it means that the truth alighted upon the hearts of the sorcerers (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whatsoever they did” means the sorcerers' deceptions; the verse joins other declarations of truth's victory over falsehood.
rows.anchor: Whatsoever they did refers to the deceptions of the sorcerers, which were shown to be false

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Both Pharaoh and the sorcerers were defeated, and Pharaoh reportedly released Moses from detention.
rows.anchor: They—that is, both Pharaoh and the sorcerers—were vanquished by Moses’ feat

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Knowing their own acts were deception, the sorcerers recognized Moses' feat as divinely sourced and immediately changed heart, humbled and amazed.
rows.anchor: Because the sorcerers knew that their own feats were mere deception, they recognized that the feat produced by Moses could only have been of Divine provenance (IK, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: The repeated casting verb suggests the sorcerers were hurled into prostration as if involuntarily, contrasting their earlier deceptive casting with submission.
rows.anchor: The use of this same verb also sharpens the contrast between their earlier “casting” of the staffs for the purposes of deception and their now “being cast” into sincere submission to God

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The sorcerers prostrated themselves as a display of utter humility and submission to God.
rows.anchor: They made themselves prostrate, in a display of utter humility and submission to God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Their expert knowledge of sorcery let them recognize its limits before Moses' divine feat, illustrating how worldly sciences can point beyond themselves to higher spiritual principles.
rows.anchor: it was the sorcerers’ advanced knowledge of their own art that allowed them to recognize that Moses’ actions were not sorcery at all

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic miracles imitate yet transcend the leading arts of their peoples: Moses' sorcery, Jesus' healing in a medical age, and Muhammad's unsurpassed eloquence among poets.
rows.anchor: each messenger was sent with miracles that demonstrated an inimitable mastery of the leading arts and sciences of the people to whom they had been sent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Lord of the worlds” is a common Quranic name for God, used repeatedly in this sūrah and in accounts of earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: The sorcerers profess belief in the Lord of the worlds, a common title for God found throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming Moses and Aaron clarifies that they submit to the One God, rather than Pharaoh, who also claimed divinity.
rows.anchor: a means of making it clear that they were prostrating to the One God, and not to Pharaoh, who also considered himself a god

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says Aaron is named because otherwise Pharaoh might interpret “Lord of Moses” as himself, since he had raised Moses as a child.
rows.anchor: if they had only mentioned “the Lord of Moses,” Pharaoh might still think that they were prostrating to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aaron is a Quranic prophet, sent at Moses' request as his companion before Pharaoh and serving as a close aide during the Israelites' desert wandering.
rows.anchor: Aaron, Moses’ brother, is also identified as a prophet in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh is outraged that the sorcerers believe in Moses before he permits it; unlike them, he dismisses Moses' feat as superior sorcery.
rows.anchor: In contrast to the sorcerers, who immediately recognized that Moses’ power came from the One God, Pharaoh considered Moses’ feat no more than a sorcerer’s trick

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Th, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Pharaoh calls the contest a plot by Moses and the sorcerers to expel Egypt's inhabitants so the Israelites could settle there.
rows.anchor: He describes the entire competition, including Moses’ victory and the sorcerers’ submission, as a plot devised by Moses and the sorcerers together

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: One report says Moses privately secured the sorcerers' promise to believe and attest to his message if he won; Pharaoh overheard and later alleged a plot.
rows.anchor: before the competition began, Moses approached the head of the sorcerers to ask if they would believe in him and witness to the truth of his message

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: Pharaoh's warning that they will soon know refers to the terrible punishment he plans to impose.
rows.anchor: that is, they will know the terrible punishment Pharaoh intends to impose on them (Th)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's threatened punishment resembles the penalty for waging war against God and His Messenger and spreading corruption.
rows.anchor: The punishment here is similar to the punishment ordained for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and endeavor to work corruption upon the earth

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Commentators report Pharaoh was the first to impose cutting opposite hands and feet followed by crucifixion.
rows.anchor: The commentators report that the first person to execute the punishment of “cutting off hands and feet on alternate sides” and crucifixion was Pharaoh

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Pharaoh crucified victims on palm trees beside the Nile; the threat's parallel in 20:71 mentions this detail.
rows.anchor: who crucified his victims on palm trees on the banks of the Nile (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Z, Bq
rows.claim: The sorcerers' return to their Lord means they now look toward meeting God with love and longing, untroubled by death and hoping for reward for their suffering.
rows.anchor: they now looked only toward the meeting with God (Z) with love and longing (Bq) and with the hope that they would be rewarded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sorcerers' charge that Pharaoh seeks vengeance merely for faith resembles a believer at Pharaoh's court and Quranic condemnations of such persecution.
rows.anchor: is similar to the words of a secret believer in Pharaoh’s court who asks Pharaoh if he would kill a man for saying, “My Lord is God”

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The signs of the Lord for which Pharaoh takes vengeance are the feats Moses performed.
rows.anchor: The signs of our Lord refers to the feats performed by Moses (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Their request for patience asks God to keep them steadfast through torture and death, lest duress return them to disbelief; the same prayer appears before Goliath's army.
rows.anchor: a request that God aid them in remaining steadfast in the face of torture and death at the hands of Pharaoh, lest they revert to disbelief under this extreme duress

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Some say the painful death purified the sorcerers of their past sins.
rows.anchor: According to some, the painful death suffered by the sorcerers purified them of their past sins (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslimīn here means submitters universally, those who fully submit to the One God.
rows.anchor: used here in the universal sense of those who submit themselves fully to the One God

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Pharaoh reportedly killed and crucified them that day; early commentators say they began as sorcerers and ended as martyrs.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh reportedly had the sorcerers killed and crucified that very day, and several early commentators observed that the sorcerers “began the day as sorcerers and ended it as martyrs”

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The final request may mean “take us to Thyself as submitters,” a plea for immediate death to escape Pharaoh's punishment.
rows.anchor: can also be translated “take us to Thyself as submitters” and might therefore be understood as a plea for God to take them to Himself immediately

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: An idolater seeking asylum is to hear the Quran and Islamic teachings, then be escorted safely until reaching home.
rows.anchor: idolaters could come and hear the Quran and the teachings of Islam and then be taken to a place of safety

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Commentators disagree whether 9:6 was abrogated by verses such as 47:4, which allows freeing prisoners or holding them for ransom; the dominant view says neither verse was abrogated.
rows.anchor: The dominant opinion, however, is that neither 9:6 nor 47:4 was abrogated

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: On the dominant view, from the start of the war years, beginning at Badr, the Prophet and believers could kill the enemy, take prisoners, or release them.
rows.anchor: the Prophet and the believers were given the authority to slay the enemy, take them prisoner, or release them from the very beginning of the years of war

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Commentators differ over how much Quran an asylum seeker must hear: some require all of it, while others limit it to this sūrah's essential message for idolaters.
rows.anchor: some saying it should be the entire Quran, others restricting it to this sūrah, since it contains the essence of what idolaters need to hear

rows.speaker: Bg, Ṭs
rows.claim: Provision from Heaven and earth refers respectively to rain and vegetation.
rows.anchor: From the Heaven and earth is understood to be a reference to rain and vegetation, respectively (Bg, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Other commentators understand provision from Heaven and earth to include both bodily and spiritual sustenance.
rows.anchor: such provision can be both bodily and spiritual (Q)

rows.speaker: Bg, Ṭs
rows.claim: Having power over hearing and sight means giving people hearing and sight.
rows.anchor: “Who gives you hearing and sight?” (Bg, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about bringing the living from the dead and dead from the living is answered in 30:19 and related passages.
rows.anchor: A response to the question, Who brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living? can be seen in 30:19

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The respondents are the Makkans, who answer “God” because His agency comes immediately to mind, especially as many viewed Allah as head of an Arab pantheon.
rows.anchor: they, namely, the Makkans (R), will say, “God”

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The call to reverence targets the Makkans' association of idols with God and warns them of their error and its coming punishment.
rows.anchor: addresses the Makkans’ seeing idols as partners with God and is meant to alert them to their current state of error and the impending punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's directing the affair is discussed at 10:3.
rows.anchor: For God’s directing the affair, see 10:3c

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: “That is God” affirms the answer to the questions in the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: That is God is an affirmation of the response provided in v. 31 (JJ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: “Your true Lord” means that no one who has thought deeply about God can doubt His Lordship.
rows.anchor: no one who has thought deeply about God can doubt His Lordship (Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The disbelievers cannot prevent God from punishing them in this life if He wishes.
rows.anchor: He wishes to do so (Z); cf. 8:59

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That God alone is humanity's protector is a recurring Quranic theme.
rows.anchor: That God is the only Protector for human beings is a common Quranic refrain

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Their punishment is multiplied because they are punished for their own misguidance and for misleading others.
rows.anchor: they will be punished for their own misguided ways and also for misguiding others (JJ)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Not hearing or seeing denotes deafness of heart and blindness of soul, spiritual insensibility to prophetic messages.
rows.anchor: Rāzī notes that these words refer to a “deafness of heart and blindness of soul,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What the disbelievers fabricated, including idols, ideas, and religious beliefs, will ultimately forsake them.
rows.anchor: one will ultimately be forsaken by what one has fabricated, including false idols, ideas, and religious beliefs

rows.speaker: Bg, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Jacob became worried when his sons arrived weeping and asked whether anything had happened to their sheep in the pasture.
rows.anchor: Jacob became worried and asked them if anything had happened to their sheep that were out in the pasture (Bg, Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Their false tears show blatant hypocrisy; total hypocrites can control their eyes and cry at will.
rows.anchor: it was their hypocrisy that allowed them to lie in such a blatant manner, saying that when people become total hypocrites, they can control their eyes to the point that they can cry at will

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: When the brothers said the sheep were unharmed, Jacob asked what had happened and where Joseph was.
rows.anchor: “What happened to you then, and where is Joseph?” (Bg)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The brothers claim they raced to train for fighting enemies and wolves that had been taking their sheep.
rows.anchor: they went racing with one another in order to train themselves so that they could combat enemies and the wolf

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: “Their things” means the brothers' garments and clothes.
rows.anchor: they had left Joseph with their things, namely, their garments and clothes (Bg)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Upon hearing Joseph was dead, Jacob fainted; the brothers poured water on him, and he remained unconscious until the next morning.
rows.anchor: Jacob fainted, and the brothers poured water over him to wake him up. Yet he remained unconscious until early the next morning (Q)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: The brothers say Jacob would not believe them even if truthful because they felt he had a bad opinion of them.
rows.anchor: they felt Jacob had a bad opinion of them (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: From Jacob's perspective, suspicion of his sons already made their story unbelievable; Genesis instead says he believed their account.
rows.anchor: From Jacob’s perspective, he could not believe them, because he was suspicious of them to begin with (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers' complaint recalls their earlier question about Jacob's distrust and foreshadows their later truthful report that he still disbelieves, partly because of their actions.
rows.anchor: This mistrust of the brothers foreshadows an incident later in this sūrah in which the brothers return to Jacob with some news about which they were actually being truthful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers took Joseph's shirt after tearing it off before throwing him into the well; Genesis describes Jacob's special robe for Joseph.
rows.anchor: The brothers had Joseph’s shirt from the moment they had torn it off him before they cast him into the well

rows.speaker: IṬ
rows.claim: Before returning at night, the brothers stained the shirt with blood from a slaughtered baby goat or lamb.
rows.anchor: for this purpose (IṬ; cf. Genesis 37:31

rows.speaker: Aj, Ṭb
rows.claim: Jacob's accusation means the brothers had persuaded themselves their deeds were not grievous, though he did not believe them.
rows.anchor: they had convinced themselves that their actions were not grievous (Aj), but that he did not believe them (Ṭb)

rows.speaker: IṬ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Jacob asks why the shirt showed no predator damage, since a wolf would have torn it apart while devouring Joseph.
rows.anchor: if a wolf had devoured Joseph, his shirt would have been completely torn apart by the wolf (IṬ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beautiful patience means patience that complains to God alone; another reading is “My patience is/will be beautiful.” It consoles grief with hope that hardship passes and patience triumphs.
rows.anchor: Beautiful patience! which refers to a kind of patience that causes one not to complain to anyone but God

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some interpret Jacob's words as “[My patience is/will be] a beautiful patience.”
rows.anchor: Some interpret it to mean, “[My patience is/will be] a beautiful patience” (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Jacob says he seeks God's help to bear the lie his sons tell about Joseph's death; he repeats the words in verse 83.
rows.anchor: means that Jacob seeks God’s Help in bearing the lie that his sons were telling him concerning Joseph’s death (Aj)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: God gives people some of what they ask verbally or what they request implicitly through need without speaking.
rows.anchor: God gives people something of all that they ask for with their tongues, or of what they ask for by being in a state of need without actually articulating it verbally (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Because mā can be read differently, some understand the verse to say God gives unrequested blessings such as the sun and moon.
rows.anchor: some read this to mean, “He gives you of that which you do not ask of Him,” referring to blessings such as the sun and the moon (Q)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Legitimate requests, excluding sin or severed family ties, are answered by granting them now, storing the reward for the Hereafter, or diverting an equivalent evil.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said that God will grant one’s legitimate requests

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: People cannot count God's blessings or thank Him for all of them.
rows.anchor: they are also unable to thank Him for all of them (Bg; see also 16:18)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of humanity as ungrateful is echoed in many verses and complements the description of humanity as an ignorant wrongdoer.
rows.anchor: Truly mankind is wrongdoing, ungrateful is complemented by the last part of 33:72

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children adorn worldly life as sources of status and security, but do not necessarily indicate divine favor, protect from punishment, or endure.
rows.anchor: Wealth and children are the adornment of this world, because they are considered a source of status and security

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteous deeds endure because they bring lasting reward in the Hereafter, as also stated in 19:76.
rows.anchor: righteous deeds “endure” in that they bring lasting reward in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Moses encountered God at night in winter after losing his way.
rows.anchor: Moses’ encounter with God occurred at night, during the winter, when Moses had lost his way (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Moses sought warmth or illumination from the fire he saw.
rows.anchor: Having seen the fire (Q), he sought warmth or perhaps some means of illumination from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire is said to have been on Horeb, the mountain of God in Exodus; it also symbolizes rising levels of spiritual certainty.
rows.anchor: It is said that the fire was on Horeb

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Al-Anbiyāʾ is a Makkan sūrah named for its many prophetic stories.
rows.anchor: a Makkan sūrah (Q), receives its name from the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening section recounts Quraysh's accusations and incredulity toward the Prophet, then recalls earlier peoples destroyed despite being unable to avert punishment.
rows.anchor: The first section recounts the various accusations of falsehood and expressions of incredulity directed at the Prophet by the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next passages reject God's having a consort or child and multiple divinities, invite reflection on the cosmos, and remind humanity of death and judgment.
rows.anchor: The impossibility of God taking a consort or having a child and the absurdity of more than one divinity in the universe are explained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A brief account mentions Moses and Aaron.
rows.anchor: After a brief mention of Moses and Aaron (vv. 48–50)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's account includes his ruse blaming the largest idol for destroying the smaller idols and his people's attempt to burn him alive.
rows.anchor: a longer account of Abraham is given

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah next recounts Lot, Noah, David and Solomon, Job, Ishmael, Idrīs, Dhu’l-Kifl, Jonah, Zachariah, John, and Mary.
rows.anchor: Ishmael, Idrīs, and Dhu’l-Kifl (vv. 85–86); Jonah (vv. 87–88)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section recalls religious communities' fragmentation, Gog and Magog, idolaters and idols in Hell, and the cosmos's destruction and renewal for the righteous.
rows.anchor: The last part of al-Anbiyāʾ addresses the end of the world and the coming of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes by calling the Prophet a mercy to all creation, noting his warning, and saying he does not know when the final doom will arrive.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is a mercy to all creation, and a reminder both that he has given fair warning of what is to come
